reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard sleep & reproductive medicine references
clinicalPearls: Central sleep apnoea reflects a transient loss of respiratory drive, so airflow and respiratory effort stop together, distinguishing it from obstructive events where effort continues against a closed airway
Unlike the loud habitual snoring of obstructive disease, patients may present chiefly with fragmented sleep, frequent awakenings, nocturnal breathlessness, or witnessed pauses without much snoring
A Cheyne-Stokes crescendo-decrescendo breathing pattern is characteristic and points strongly towards underlying heart failure
The disorder clusters into hypercapnic forms (blunted drive, as in brainstem disease or opioid use) and non-hypercapnic forms driven by an unstable, oversensitive ventilatory control loop
Polysomnography is required to confirm the diagnosis and to separate central from obstructive and mixed events

Treatment is directed at the underlying cause; optimising heart failure therapy often reduces central events, and supplemental oxygen or adaptive ventilatory support may be considered in selected patients
Long-term opioid therapy is an increasingly common and reversible contributor that should be actively sought in the history
Adaptive servo-ventilation should be used cautiously and is contraindicated in patients with symptomatic heart failure and reduced ejection fraction
reference.pathophysiology: Central sleep apnoea arises from intermittent failure of the brainstem respiratory rhythm generator to signal the respiratory muscles, so both airflow and inspiratory effort cease simultaneously. In non-hypercapnic (high loop gain) forms, ventilatory control is unstable: an oversensitive chemoreceptor response drives arterial CO2 below the apnoeic threshold, breathing stops until CO2 rises again, and overshoot perpetuates a cyclical pattern. Prolonged circulation time in heart failure delays chemoreceptor feedback and produces the crescendo-decrescendo Cheyne-Stokes cycling. In hypercapnic forms, reduced central drive or neuromuscular capacity (brainstem lesions, opioids, chronic hypoventilation) causes sustained underventilation with superimposed central pauses. Recurrent apnoeas generate cyclical hypoxaemia, arousals, and sympathetic surges.
additionalDifferentials: Nocturnal breathlessness from decompensated heart failure
additionalInvestigations: Attended polysomnography to characterise and quantify central versus obstructive events
Echocardiography and cardiac assessment when heart failure is suspected
Daytime arterial or capillary blood gas to identify chronic hypercapnia
Brain and brainstem imaging if a central neurological cause is suspected
Review of opioid and sedative medication as a reversible contributor
redFlags: Cheyne-Stokes breathing indicating underlying heart failure requiring cardiac evaluation and optimisation
New central apnoea with focal neurology suggesting a brainstem lesion or stroke
Central events emerging or worsening on chronic opioid therapy
Daytime hypercapnia, cor pulmonale, or morning headache signalling chronic ventilatory failure
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is largely determined by the underlying disorder; central sleep apnoea complicating advanced heart failure is a marker of poorer outcome, whereas apnoea from reversible causes such as opioids or high altitude often improves once the trigger is addressed.
pitfalls: Assuming all sleep apnoea is obstructive and missing the absent respiratory effort that defines central events
Prescribing adaptive servo-ventilation to patients with symptomatic reduced-ejection-fraction heart failure, in whom it may be harmful
Overlooking chronic opioid use as a treatable cause
Failing to investigate and treat underlying heart failure or brainstem pathology
